cr.tip.goodCap: 💡 Sandwich an enemy piece along a row or column to capture it. Only the mover captures, so stepping between two enemies is safe.
cr.tip.missEsc: 💡 As the defenders, check every move whether the king has an open path to a corner (or an edge).
cr.tip.missKill: 💡 Of the four squares around the king (three next to the throne), look for a piece that can reach the last one.
cr.tip.allowEsc: 💡 Attackers stay safe by keeping a piece on every line the king could run along. Guarding the three squares around each corner is the basics.
cr.tip.allowCapK: 💡 Three attackers around the king is a red alert: block the last square so no attacker can reach it.
cr.tip.missCap: 💡 Before moving, ask “can I sandwich that piece?” Corners and the empty throne also act as the other side of the sandwich.
cr.tip.allowCap: 💡 After your move, check both neighbours along rows and columns: can the opponent put a piece on the other side?
cr.tip.allowFork: 💡 A square where the king opens two paths at once is the most dangerous square for the attackers. Block it in advance.
cr.tip.gen: 💡 The arrow on the board is the best move; the numbers are the values of the moves.
rl.title: Learn the rules
intro.hist: Tafl games were the board battles of the Vikings; boards and pieces have been found in Scandinavia, Iceland and the British Isles. The best known is Hnefatafl, “the king's table”, where one side protects its king. Chess pushed it aside in the Middle Ages, but it was reconstructed in the 20th century, largely from Tablut, recorded by Linnaeus in Lapland in 1732. Today the Copenhagen rules are the standard of international tournaments.
intro.win: The defenders win by bringing their king to any corner. The attackers win by surrounding the king on four sides. All pieces move like a chess rook, and an enemy piece is captured by sandwiching it between two of yours. It is an uneven battle: 24 attackers against 12 defenders and a king.
intro.cult: Icelandic sagas mention tafl being played, and glass and bone pieces have come out of Norwegian and Swedish graves. Today the game is played most of all in Denmark and Britain, with online and over-the-board tournaments almost every year. The small Brandubh is known as an Irish game, and Tablut as the game of Lapland.
tr.board.b: The king and 12 defenders start in the middle of an 11×11 board, the 24 attackers on the four sides. The attackers move first. The central throne and the four corners (gold rings) are special: only the king may stop on them.
tr.move.b: Every piece moves any number of squares in a straight line, along a row or a column (like a rook in chess). Pieces never jump over others.
tr.move.task: Move one of the defenders (white) along a row or a column.
tr.move.ok: That's it! Pieces slide straight, as far as the squares are empty.
tr.capture.b: Put an enemy piece between two of your pieces on a row or a column and it is captured. Only the side that moves captures. The king helps to capture too.
tr.capture.task: Capture an attacker (black) by sandwiching it.
tr.capture.ok: Captured! That is the basic capture of tafl.
tr.capture.ng: Move so that an enemy piece is between two of yours.
tr.hostile.b: The corners act like an enemy piece for both sides, and so does the empty throne. A piece next to a corner is captured with just one piece on its other side.
tr.hostile.task: Use the corner to capture the attacker.
tr.hostile.ok: The square next to a corner is dangerous. The corner served as the wall!
tr.hostile.ng: Sandwich the attacker next to the corner between the corner and your piece.
tr.safe.b: A piece that moves between two enemy pieces is not captured (only the side that closes the sandwich captures). The white piece in the picture stands between two black ones, but it is safe.
tr.escape.b: If the king reaches any corner, the defenders win.
tr.escape.task: Bring the king to a corner.
tr.escape.ng: Move the king all the way to a corner.
tr.kingcap.b: The king is captured when attackers surround it on all four sides (next to the throne: three sides and the throne). A king on the edge cannot be captured.
tr.kingcap.task: Capture the king with the attackers (black).
tr.kingcap.ok: The king is captured! The attackers win.
tr.kingcap.ng: Put an attacker on the one free square next to the king.
tr.edge.t: Shieldwall: capturing a row on the edge
tr.edge.b: Two or more pieces in a row on the edge are captured together when both ends are closed and each of them has an enemy in front (a corner can close an end; a king in the row is not captured). In the picture, black moves to a9 and captures both white pieces.
tr.fort.b: If the king is on the edge, can still move, and sits in a fort of defenders that can never be broken, the defenders win. The king in the picture can shuttle between a4 and a3, and none of the white pieces around can ever be captured.
tr.ends.b: If the attackers enclose every defender so that none can reach the edge, the attackers win. A side that cannot move loses. The same position three times is a loss for the defenders (they cannot escape by repeating moves). 200 moves without a capture is a draw.
tr.variants.b: Brandubh (7×7): 8 attackers, 4 defenders and the king. Away from the throne the king is captured by just two pieces. Tablut (9×9): 16 attackers, 8 defenders and the king. The king escapes on any edge square; away from the throne it is captured by two.
rt.title: Your rating
rt.desc: An AI opponent (15 kyu to 5 dan) is chosen to match your rating (starting at 1000) — usually one of similar strength, sometimes stronger or weaker. Your side is random; the defenders' small edge is taken into account in the expected score. Win to go up, lose to go down (Elo; the first 10 games move more). Copenhagen rules, 7 minutes + 4 seconds per move. No undo, hints or evaluation during the game.
rt.noEval: No evaluation during a rated game
rt.abandonQ: A rated game is in progress. Leaving now abandons it and counts as a loss. Continue?
ls.title: Lessons
ls.desc: “First steps” for players who just learned the rules, “Tactics” that decide games, “Strategy” for each side, and the “Variants” of the small boards. Five problems per step, 20 points each; 75 points to pass. All problems are checked by the engine; in the strategy problems, moves other than the best also score by how little they lose.
fb.values: Engine values (one attacker = 1.0): your move {a} / best {b}
course.basics.sub: Start here once you know the rules: moving, capturing, letting the king escape and capturing the king, checked with problems.
course.tactics.sub: The shieldwall, two escape paths at once (tuichi), blocking the king's paths, the edge fort and the encirclement — the patterns that decide games.
course.strategy.sub: The attackers seal the corners and close the ring; the defenders open lanes and let the king run. Scored by how close your move is to the engine's.
course.variants.sub: Brandubh on 7×7 and Tablut on 9×9: a weaker king and other escape squares, checked with problems.
course.graduate: 🎉 You finished “First steps” and are ready to play! Try the AI at 15–10 kyu first, playing the defenders.
op.title: Openings (opening plans)
op.desc: Typical opening plans under the Copenhagen rules. The first moves show the plan; the rest of each line was chosen by this site's engine after a deep search. Step through it with “Study”, then guess the engine's moves in “Practice” (5 problems, 75 points to pass).
op.credit: The plans and lines were chosen by this site's engine (a few seconds per position) and checked to keep the opening close to even. They are not necessarily the names used in human tournaments.
op.studyDesc: A typical line of {n} moves, one move at a time with comments
op.practiceDesc: 5 problems from this opening: 20 points for the best move, partial points for close ones

op.grp.att.sub: Moving first, the attackers guard the corners before the king can run, then tighten the ring step by step.
op.grp.def.sub: The defenders bring pieces out to open gaps in the attackers' ring and clear lanes for the king.
pz.title: Tafl puzzles
pz.desc: “Escape with the king in N” and “Capture the king in N”. The opponent answers with its most stubborn move. There is exactly one correct first move, and every puzzle is solved and checked by the engine.

rule.copenhagen.d: 11×11, 24 attackers. The king is taken on four sides and escapes to a corner. The tournament standard.
rule.brandubh.d: 7×7, 8 attackers. Even the king is taken by two — a short, sharp Irish board.
rule.tablut.d: 9×9, 16 attackers. The king escapes on any edge — the Lapland game recorded by Linnaeus.
